nameStory: The Persian silk tree gets its name from its incredibly soft, silky flower clusters that feel like fine thread when you touch them. It's called 'Persian' because it was first introduced to the West from the regions around ancient Persia, though it's also native to other parts of Asia. The delicate, wispy flowers really do look and feel like pink silk pompoms dancing in the breeze.
description: The Persian silk tree is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree that looks almost tropical with its feathery, fern-like leaves and fluffy pink flowers. It typically grows 20-25 feet tall with a broad, spreading crown that's often wider than it is tall. The tree has a graceful, umbrella-like shape with delicate foliage that creates dappled shade, making it look quite exotic among New England's native trees. Despite its delicate appearance, it's surprisingly hardy and can thrive in our region's climate.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Stunning pink pompom-like clusters that feel incredibly soft and silky to the touch, blooming from late spring into summer. Each flower head is made up of many tiny flowers with long, thread-like stamens that create the fluffy appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, fern-like compound leaves that fold up at night and in cold weather, similar to a sensitive plant. Each leaf is made up of many tiny leaflets that give the tree an almost tropical, delicate appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, papery seed pods that are tan to brown and persist through winter, containing several hard seeds. The pods are typical of the legume family and rattle when shaken.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young that becomes slightly furrowed with age, but never deeply ridged like many native trees. The bark feels relatively smooth to the touch even on mature trees.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctive umbrella or vase-like shape with multiple trunks or low-branching habit, creating a broad, flat-topped crown. Often wider than it is tall, with gracefully arching branches.

habitat: Persian silk trees are most commonly found in disturbed areas, along roadsides, and in suburban settings where they've escaped cultivation. They prefer well-drained soils and full sun, often establishing in abandoned lots, forest edges, and areas with poor soil where many native trees struggle. In New England, they're more frequent in warmer, southern areas and urban heat islands.

seasonality.spring: Delicate fern-like leaves emerge late in spring, often after most native trees have leafed out. The distinctive compound leaves are a key identifying feature even before flowers appear.
seasonality.summer: Spectacular pink silk-puff flowers bloom from June through August, making this the easiest time for identification. The flowers have a light, sweet fragrance and attract butterflies and hummingbirds.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the flat seed pods develop and mature to brown. Fall color is not particularly showy compared to native trees.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic umbrella shape, and brown papery seed pods often persist on the tree, rattling in winter winds. The smooth gray bark and distinctive branching pattern help with identification.

funFact: The Persian silk tree's leaves actually go to sleep at night, folding up in a behavior called 'nyctinasty' - if you check on one after dark, you'll see the feathery leaflets have closed up tight, then they'll reopen with the morning sun just like a person waking up and stretching!
confusionNotes: Persian silk tree is sometimes confused with native locust trees, but locusts have white flowers and much more deeply grooved bark. Remember: pink pompom flowers and smooth bark mean silk tree, white flower clusters and deeply furrowed bark mean locust.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'mimosa tree' by many people, true mimosas are different plants entirely. This naming confusion is common in the southern United States where Persian silk trees are more established. It's also worth knowing that while beautiful, this is considered an invasive species in many areas and can crowd out native plants.
compareHints: Since Persian silk tree is the only Albizia species commonly found in New England, compare it to other legume family trees like black locust or honey locust. Unlike these natives, Persian silk tree has much more delicate, fern-like foliage and distinctively soft pink flowers rather than white or greenish ones. The overall growth form is also more graceful and umbrella-like compared to the more upright growth of native locusts.
